claim: Complex cognition relies on flexible working memory, which is severely limited in its capacity.
source: Complex cognition relies on flexible working memory, which is severely limited in its capacity.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about working memory.

claim: The neuronal computations underlying working memory capacity limits have been extensively studied in humans and in monkeys, resulting in competing theoretical models.
source: The neuronal computations underlying these capacity limits have been extensively studied in humans and in monkeys, resulting in competing theoretical models.
evidence: This refers to existing body of research in the field.

claim: Neuronal encoding and maintenance of information in crow NCL were affected by item load in a way virtually identical to results obtained from monkey prefrontal cortex.
source: We found that neuronal encoding and maintenance of information were affected by item load, in a way that is virtually identical to results obtained from monkey prefrontal cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data comparing crows and monkeys.

claim: Contemporary neurophysiological models of working memory employ divisive normalization as an important mechanism that may result in the capacity limitation.
source: Contemporary neurophysiological models of working memory employ divisive normalization as an important mechanism that may result in the capacity limitation.
evidence: This refers to existing theoretical models in the literature.

claim: Carrion crows and macaque monkeys share divisive normalization as a neuronal computation that is in line with mammalian models.
source: Here, we report that carrion crows and macaque monkeys share divisive normalization as a neuronal computation that is in line with mammalian models.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Computational models of working memory developed in the mammalian cortex can also apply to non-cortical associative brain regions of birds.
source: This indicates that computational models of working memory developed in the mammalian cortex can also apply to non-cortical associative brain regions of birds.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings about divisive normalization in crows.

claim: Working memory can hold information for a short period of time to allow further processing in the absence of sensory input.
source: Working memory (WM) can hold information for a short period of time to allow further processing in the absence of sensory input (Cowan, 2017; Oberauer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Working memory is a cornerstone for complex cognition by bridging the gap between the immediate sensory environment and behavior.
source: By bridging this gap between the immediate sensory environment and behavior, WM is a cornerstone for complex cognition.
evidence: This is a conceptual statement based on established understanding of working memory function.

claim: Working memory is a very flexible memory system, yet severely limited in its capacity.
source: It is a very flexible memory system, yet severely limited in its capacity.
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of working memory.

claim: For simple stimuli like colors, the working memory capacity is very similar between humans, monkeys, and crows.
source: While this capacity is often seen as a general cognitive bottleneck, for simple stimuli, like colors, the capacity is very similar between humans, monkeys, and crows (Balakhonov and Rose, 2017; Buschman et al., 2011; Cowan, 2001; Luck and Vogel, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Discrete models of working memory argue that a fixed number of items can be stored, and once capacity is reached, an additional item can only be maintained if it replaces a previous item.
source: 'Discrete models' of WM argue that a fixed number of items can be stored. Once this capacity is reached, an additional item can only be maintained if it replaces a previous item (Awh et al., 2007; Fukuda et al., 2010; Luck and Vogel, 1997; Vogel and Machizawa, 2004; Zhang and Luck, 2008).
evidence: This describes a theoretical model supported by citations.

claim: Continuous models describe working memory as a flexible resource that is allocated to individual items, with a minimum amount required for successful retention, thereby resulting in a capacity limit.
source: 'Continuous models' describe WM as a flexible resource that is allocated to individual items. A minimum amount of this resource has to be allocated to each item for successful retention, thereby resulting in a capacity limit (Bays and Husain, 2008; van den Berg et al., 2012; Wilken and Ma, 2004).
evidence: This describes a theoretical model supported by citations.

claim: Neurophysiological models of working memory capacity suggest that interference between memory representations within the neuronal network is a source of information loss and capacity limitation.
source: On the neurophysiological level, models of WM capacity suggest that interference between memory representations ('items') within the neuronal network is a source of information loss and capacity limitation (Bouchacourt and Buschman, 2019; Lundqvist et al., 2016; Lundqvist et al., 2011; Schneegans et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical models.

claim: Interference in working memory may arise due to divisive normalization that appears as competition between items, related to oscillatory dynamics, WM flexibility, and neuronal information sampling.
source: Interference may arise due to divisive normalization that appears as competition between items, related to oscillatory dynamics (Lundqvist et al., 2016; Lundqvist et al., 2011), WM flexibility (Bouchacourt and Buschman, 2019), and neuronal information sampling (Schneegans et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific mechanisms in the literature.

claim: Divisive normalization is a computational principle that normalizes neuronal responses by creating a ratio between the response of an individual neuron and the summed activity of a pool of neurons.
source: Divisive normalization is a computational principle that acts upon neurons when presenting multiple stimuli simultaneously, it normalizes neuronal responses by creating 'a ratio between the response of an individual neuron and the summed activity of a pool of neurons' (Carandini and Heeger, 2011, p. 51).
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation.

claim: When two stimuli are presented simultaneously within the receptive field of a visual sensory neuron, the neuron's firing rate becomes normalized by the populations' responses to each individual stimulus.
source: An effect related to divisive normalization can be observed when two stimuli are presented either individually or simultaneously within the receptive field of a visual sensory neuron. The neuron's firing rate when the stimuli are presented simultaneously becomes normalized by the populations' responses to each individual stimulus (Carandini et al., 1997; Heeger, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Normalization of neuronal responses is commonly observed in many species throughout the animal kingdom, not just in sensory, but also in cognitive domains.
source: Normalization of neuronal responses is commonly observed in many species throughout the animal kingdom, not just in sensory, but also in cognitive domains (Carandini and Heeger, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Crows have a similar limit in working memory capacity to monkeys.
source: Crows have a similar limit in WM capacity and neuronal correlates of WM are comparable to monkeys' (Balakhonov and Rose, 2017; Nieder, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Neuronal correlates of working memory in crows are comparable to monkeys.
source: Crows have a similar limit in WM capacity and neuronal correlates of WM are comparable to monkeys' (Balakhonov and Rose, 2017; Nieder, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The neuronal architecture of sensory areas is similar between birds and mammals.
source: But while the neuronal architecture of sensory areas is similar between birds and mammals, higher associative areas, critical for WM, do not share a common architecture between the species (Stacho et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a comparative neuroanatomy study.

claim: Higher associative areas critical for working memory do not share a common architecture between birds and mammals.
source: But while the neuronal architecture of sensory areas is similar between birds and mammals, higher associative areas, critical for WM, do not share a common architecture between the species (Stacho et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a comparative neuroanatomy study.

claim: The avian forebrain structure nidopallium caudolaterale (NCL) is a critical component of avian working memory.
source: The avian forebrain structure, nidopallium caudolaterale (NCL) is a critical component of avian WM.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about avian neuroanatomy and function.

claim: The NCL is considered functionally equivalent to the mammalian prefrontal cortex.
source: The NCL is considered functionally equivalent to the mammalian prefrontal cortex (PFC) (Güntürkün and Bugnyar, 2016; Nieder, 2017), as it receives projections from all sensory modalities (Kröner and Güntürkün, 1999), projects to premotor areas (Kröner and Güntürkün, 1999), and is a target of dopaminergic innervation (Waldmann and Güntürkün, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing anatomical and functional properties.

claim: The NCL receives projections from all sensory modalities.
source: The NCL is considered functionally equivalent to the mammalian prefrontal cortex (PFC) (Güntürkün and Bugnyar, 2016; Nieder, 2017), as it receives projections from all sensory modalities (Kröner and Güntürkün, 1999), projects to premotor areas (Kröner and Güntürkün, 1999), and is a target of dopaminergic innervation (Waldmann and Güntürkün, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an anatomical study.

claim: The NCL projects to premotor areas.
source: The NCL is considered functionally equivalent to the mammalian prefrontal cortex (PFC) (Güntürkün and Bugnyar, 2016; Nieder, 2017), as it receives projections from all sensory modalities (Kröner and Güntürkün, 1999), projects to premotor areas (Kröner and Güntürkün, 1999), and is a target of dopaminergic innervation (Waldmann and Güntürkün, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an anatomical study.

claim: The NCL is a target of dopaminergic innervation.
source: The NCL is considered functionally equivalent to the mammalian prefrontal cortex (PFC) (Güntürkün and Bugnyar, 2016; Nieder, 2017), as it receives projections from all sensory modalities (Kröner and Güntürkün, 1999), projects to premotor areas (Kröner and Güntürkün, 1999), and is a target of dopaminergic innervation (Waldmann and Güntürkün, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a neurochemical study.

claim: Behavioral performance in the working memory task was influenced by the number of colored squares on the screen.
source: The behavioral performance was influenced by the number of colored squares on the screen.
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Performance significantly decreased with an increasing number of ipsilateral squares (median performances, load 1: 95.88%, load 2: 78.31%, load 3: 58.21%; Friedman test: Χ² = 92.00, p < 0.001).
source: It significantly decreased with an increasing number of ipsilateral squares (median performances, load 1: 95.88%, load 2: 78.31%, load 3: 58.21%; Friedman test: Χ² = 92.00, p < 0.001, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The number of ipsilateral colors significantly reduced performance (βipsi –0.177, t(459) = –18.00, p < 0.001).
source: We found that the number of ipsilateral colors significantly reduced performance (βipsi –0.177, t(459) = –18.00, p < 0.001), whereas the number of contralateral colors did not (βcontra –0.021, t(459) = –1.77, p = 0.0772; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by generalized linear model analysis and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The number of contralateral colors did not significantly affect performance (βcontra –0.021, t(459) = –1.77, p = 0.0772).
source: We found that the number of ipsilateral colors significantly reduced performance (βipsi –0.177, t(459) = –18.00, p < 0.001), whereas the number of contralateral colors did not (βcontra –0.021, t(459) = –1.77, p = 0.0772; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by generalized linear model analysis and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There was a significant interaction between ipsilateral and contralateral load (β = –0.024, t(458) = –4.28, p < 0.001).
source: There was also a significant interaction between ipsilateral and contralateral load (β = –0.024, t(458) = –4.28, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is supported by generalized linear model analysis.

claim: Contralateral load by itself did not significantly affect performance.
source: Therefore, we conclude that contralateral load by itself did not significantly affect performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing full and reduced statistical models.

claim: The capacity K peaks at four items (mean ± SEM: 3.05±.038).
source: The capacity K peaks at four items (mean ± SEM: 3.05±.038, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is calculated from behavioral data and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The behavioral observations in crows are very similar to observations made in primates.
source: These observations are very similar to observations made in primates (Buschman et al., 2011) and fully reproduce our earlier behavioral findings (Balakhonov and Rose, 2017).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: 362 neurons were recorded from the NCL of two crows performing the working memory task.
source: We recorded 362 neurons from the NCL of two crows performing the WM task (delayed change localization).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data collection.

claim: All reported effects were present in each individual bird.
source: All reported effects were also present in each individual bird (Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2), we, therefore, pooled the data for population analysis.
evidence: This is stated and supported by supplementary figures.

claim: A large subset of neurons responded to the presence of a color by substantially increasing or decreasing their firing rate relative to baseline.
source: A large subset of neurons responded to the presence of a color (i.e., at load 1) by substantially increasing or decreasing their firing rate relative to baseline.
evidence: This is an observation from the neuronal recording data.

claim: The change in firing rate occurred selectively, depending on the presented color either in the sample or the delay period.
source: This change in firing rate occurred selectively, depending on the presented color either in the sample (Figure 2A) or the delay period (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the neuronal recording data shown in figures.

claim: For most neurons, the difference in firing rate between the two possible colors became attenuated when the load increased from one to two colors, and was further attenuated from two to three colors.
source: For most neurons, this difference in firing rate between the two possible colors became attenuated when the load increased from one to two colors, and it was further attenuated from two to three colors.
evidence: This is an observation from the neuronal recording data analysis.

claim: Most neurons did not sustain information about color throughout the entire sample or memory delay but rather had shorter periods in which the information was significant.
source: Most neurons did not sustain information about color (measured as a significant PEV, henceforth 'information') throughout the entire sample or memory delay but rather had shorter periods in which the information was significant (Figure 2A bottom).
evidence: This is an observation from the neuronal recording data analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The neuronal population can be best described by seven individual clusters.
source: We found a total of seven clusters that were organized into two overarching groups (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Group 1 contained neurons (n = 227) that showed peak information during the sample and early delay phase.
source: Group 1 contained neurons (n = 227) that showed peak information during the sample and early delay phase, while group 2 contained neurons (n = 135) that showed peak information during the delay phase.
evidence: This is a result from hierarchical clustering analysis.

claim: Group 2 contained neurons (n = 135) that showed peak information during the delay phase.
source: Group 1 contained neurons (n = 227) that showed peak information during the sample and early delay phase, while group 2 contained neurons (n = 135) that showed peak information during the delay phase.
evidence: This is a result from hierarchical clustering analysis.

claim: 37.57% (n = 136) of neurons were significant during the sample phase.
source: Overall, 37.57% (n = 136) of neurons were significant during the sample phase, 9.39% (n = 34) of neurons were significant during the memory delay, and 14.64% (n = 53) of neurons were significant during both the sample phase and the memory delay (all proportions of neurons were significantly higher than expected by chance [binomial test, see Materials and methods, all p < 0.001]).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of neuronal significance.

claim: 9.39% (n = 34) of neurons were significant during the memory delay.
source: Overall, 37.57% (n = 136) of neurons were significant during the sample phase, 9.39% (n = 34) of neurons were significant during the memory delay, and 14.64% (n = 53) of neurons were significant during both the sample phase and the memory delay (all proportions of neurons were significantly higher than expected by chance [binomial test, see Materials and methods, all p < 0.001]).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of neuronal significance.

claim: 14.64% (n = 53) of neurons were significant during both the sample phase and the memory delay.
source: Overall, 37.57% (n = 136) of neurons were significant during the sample phase, 9.39% (n = 34) of neurons were significant during the memory delay, and 14.64% (n = 53) of neurons were significant during both the sample phase and the memory delay (all proportions of neurons were significantly higher than expected by chance [binomial test, see Materials and methods, all p < 0.001]).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of neuronal significance.

claim: All proportions of significant neurons were significantly higher than expected by chance (binomial test, all p < 0.001).
source: Overall, 37.57% (n = 136) of neurons were significant during the sample phase, 9.39% (n = 34) of neurons were significant during the memory delay, and 14.64% (n = 53) of neurons were significant during both the sample phase and the memory delay (all proportions of neurons were significantly higher than expected by chance [binomial test, see Materials and methods, all p < 0.001]).
evidence: This is a result from statistical testing.

claim: Many neurons that did not have significant information at load 1 did have significant information at load 2 and load 3.
source: We found that many of the neurons that did not have significant information at load 1 did have significant information at load 2 and load 3 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an observation from the neuronal data analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: For the memory delay, more than half of the significant neurons were only significant for either load 2 or load 3, compared to only 36% of neurons that were significant at load 1.
source: For the memory delay, more than half of the significant neurons we detected were only significant for either load 2 or load 3, compared to only 36% of neurons that were significant at load 1 (Figure 3C middle).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the neuronal data analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A total of 249 (68.78%) sample neurons and 94 (25.97%) delay neurons were found by including higher loads in the analysis.
source: By including the higher loads in our analysis, we found a total of 249 (68.78%) sample neurons and 94 (25.97%) delay neurons.
evidence: This is a result from the extended neuronal data analysis.

claim: The neuronal population as a whole sustained color information throughout the entire trial.
source: The clustering analysis indicated that the population of neurons as a whole did sustain the color information throughout the entire trial (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the clustering analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: After the onset of the stimulus array, the average information exhibited a sharp increase that peaked roughly 400 ms after stimulus onset and remained at an elevated level throughout the memory delay.
source: After the onset of the stimulus array, the average information exhibited a sharp increase that peaked roughly 400 ms after stimulus onset and remained at an elevated level throughout the memory delay, until the choice array appeared.
evidence: This is an observation from the population-level neuronal data analysis.

claim: There was a strong effect of ipsilateral load on the information maintenance, with a sharp drop in information when the load increased from one item to two items.
source: Parallel to the behavioral results and in line with the results from monkeys, we found a strong effect of ipsilateral load on the information maintenance, as there was a sharp drop in information when the load increased from one item to two items (Figure 4A, blue and yellow curves).
evidence: This is an observation from the population-level neuronal data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The addition of a third item only slightly decreased the maintained information further.
source: The addition of a third item only slightly decreased the maintained information further (Figure 4A, red curve).
evidence: This is an observation from the population-level neuronal data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The load dependence was much more pronounced during the sample period than during the memory delay where the information remained at a lower elevated level.
source: The load dependence was much more pronounced during the sample period than during the memory delay where the information remained at a lower elevated level.
evidence: This is an observation from the population-level neuronal data analysis.

claim: The load effect was only present for ipsilateral manipulations; if the number of items on the contralateral side was increased, the information encoded about the colors at the favorite location did not change.
source: Notably, the load effect was only present for ipsilateral manipulations. If the number of items on the contralateral side was increased, the information encoded about the colors at the favorite location did not change (Figure 4A, right).
evidence: This is an observation from the population-level neuronal data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There was a significant drop in information with an increase in load from one through three in the early sample period (F(2,537) = 18.73, p < 0.001, ω² = 0.0616).
source: We did find a significant drop in information with an increase in load from one through three in the early (F(2,537) = 18.73, p < 0.001, ω² = 0.0616) and late (F(2,536) = 20.07, p < 0.001, ω² = 0.0661) sample period and the early (F(2,267) = 6.88, p = 0.0012, ω² = 0.0417) and late (F(2,267) = 3.85, p = 0.0225, ω² = 0.0207) delay period (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There was a significant drop in information with an increase in load from one through three in the late sample period (F(2,536) = 20.07, p < 0.001, ω² = 0.0661).
source: We did find a significant drop in information with an increase in load from one through three in the early (F(2,537) = 18.73, p < 0.001, ω² = 0.0616) and late (F(2,536) = 20.07, p < 0.001, ω² = 0.0661) sample period and the early (F(2,267) = 6.88, p = 0.0012, ω² = 0.0417) and late (F(2,267) = 3.85, p = 0.0225, ω² = 0.0207) delay period (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There was a significant drop in information with an increase in load from one through three in the early delay period (F(2,267) = 6.88, p = 0.0012, ω² = 0.0417).
source: We did find a significant drop in information with an increase in load from one through three in the early (F(2,537) = 18.73, p < 0.001, ω² = 0.0616) and late (F(2,536) = 20.07, p < 0.001, ω² = 0.0661) sample period and the early (F(2,267) = 6.88, p = 0.0012, ω² = 0.0417) and late (F(2,267) = 3.85, p = 0.0225, ω² = 0.0207) delay period (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There was a significant drop in information with an increase in load from one through three in the late delay period (F(2,267) = 3.85, p = 0.0225, ω² = 0.0207).
source: We did find a significant drop in information with an increase in load from one through three in the early (F(2,537) = 18.73, p < 0.001, ω² = 0.0616) and late (F(2,536) = 20.07, p < 0.001, ω² = 0.0661) sample period and the early (F(2,267) = 6.88, p = 0.0012, ω² = 0.0417) and late (F(2,267) = 3.85, p = 0.0225, ω² = 0.0207) delay period (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There was a large and significant drop in information between one and two items in early and late sample periods (post hoc Bonferroni corrected multiple comparisons: p < 0.001).
source: There was a large and significant drop between one and two items (post hoc Bonferroni corrected multiple comparisons: early and late sample p < 0.001, early delay p < 0.001, late delay p = 0.0198) and one and three items (post hoc Bonferroni corrected multiple comparisons: early and late sample p < 0.001, early delay p = 0.019, late delay p > 0.05) but no difference between loads 2 and 3 (post hoc Bonferroni corrected multiple comparisons: all p > 0.05).
evidence: This is a result from post hoc statistical testing.

claim: There was no difference in information between loads 2 and 3 (post hoc Bonferroni corrected multiple comparisons: all p > 0.05).
source: There was a large and significant drop between one and two items (post hoc Bonferroni corrected multiple comparisons: early and late sample p < 0.001, early delay p < 0.001, late delay p = 0.0198) and one and three items (post hoc Bonferroni corrected multiple comparisons: early and late sample p < 0.001, early delay p = 0.019, late delay p > 0.05) but no difference between loads 2 and 3 (post hoc Bonferroni corrected multiple comparisons: all p > 0.05).
evidence: This is a result from post hoc statistical testing.

claim: A significant amount of information was maintained at higher loads, even for three items.
source: The maintenance of a significant amount of information at higher loads (even for three items, early sample t(156) = 7.55, p < 0.001; late sample t(156) = 8.73, p < 0.001; early delay t(87) = 3.84, p < 0.001; late delay t(87) = 4.73, p < 0.001) and its gradual reduction when items were added to the corresponding hemifield are indicative of a flexible resource allocation and not an all-or-nothing slot-like WM.
evidence: This is a result from statistical testing and interpretation.

claim: The gradual reduction of information when items were added to the corresponding hemifield is indicative of a flexible resource allocation and not an all-or-nothing slot-like working memory.
source: The maintenance of a significant amount of information at higher loads (even for three items, early sample t(156) = 7.55, p < 0.001; late sample t(156) = 8.73, p < 0.001; early delay t(87) = 3.84, p < 0.001; late delay t(87) = 4.73, p < 0.001) and its gradual reduction when items were added to the corresponding hemifield are indicative of a flexible resource allocation and not an all-or-nothing slot-like WM.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data pattern.

claim: In error trials, the amount of information in the early and late sample phase remained above zero at load 2 and load 3.
source: The amount of information in the early and late sample phase remained above zero (load 2: early, t(186) = 3.25, p = 0.0014; late, t(186) = 5.33, p < 0.001; load 3: t(156) = 4.21, p < 0.001; Figure 4B asterisks), and was significantly smaller than in correct trials (load 2: late, t(186) = 2.81, p = 0.0055, d = 0.26; load 3: late t(156) = 2.55, p = 0.0117, d = 0.23).
evidence: This is a result from error trial analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In error trials, the amount of information was significantly smaller than in correct trials at load 2 and load 3.
source: The amount of information in the early and late sample phase remained above zero (load 2: early, t(186) = 3.25, p = 0.0014; late, t(186) = 5.33, p < 0.001; load 3: t(156) = 4.21, p < 0.001; Figure 4B asterisks), and was significantly smaller than in correct trials (load 2: late, t(186) = 2.81, p = 0.0055, d = 0.26; load 3: late t(156) = 2.55, p = 0.0117, d = 0.23).
evidence: This is a result from error trial analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There was no further maintenance of information throughout the memory delay at any load in error trials.
source: Additionally, there was no further maintenance throughout the memory delay at any load (Figure 4B, PEV at loads 2 and 3 in error trials delay, all non-significant).
evidence: This is a result from error trial analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A failure to report which color had changed at higher loads resulted from a smaller amount of information encoding during the sample phase that was not maintained throughout the delay.
source: This indicates that a failure to report which color had changed at higher loads (two and three ipsilateral items) resulted from a smaller amount of information encoding during the sample phase that was not maintained throughout the delay.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the error trial data.

claim: Divisive normalization-like regularization was observable for neurons with significant information at load 1.
source: We, therefore, hypothesized that DNR was observable for neurons with significant information at load 1.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested and confirmed by the data analysis.

claim: Information-carrying sample neurons had a fitted slope of 0.47 (R2adj 0.39, F(1,838) = 547.69, p < 0.001, CI = [0.43 0.51]).
source: Information-carrying sample neurons had a fitted slope of 0.47 (R2adj 0.39, F(1,838) = 547.69, p < 0.001, CI = [0.43 0.51]) and delay neurons had a slope of 0.50 (R2adj 0.34, F(1,342) = 175.60, p < 0.001, CI = [0.43 0.58]).
evidence: This is a result from regression analysis of divisive normalization.

claim: Information-carrying delay neurons had a slope of 0.50 (R2adj 0.34, F(1,342) = 175.60, p < 0.001, CI = [0.43 0.58]).
source: Information-carrying sample neurons had a fitted slope of 0.47 (R2adj 0.39, F(1,838) = 547.69, p < 0.001, CI = [0.43 0.51]) and delay neurons had a slope of 0.50 (R2adj 0.34, F(1,342) = 175.60, p < 0.001, CI = [0.43 0.58]).
evidence: This is a result from regression analysis of divisive normalization.

claim: The slopes of information-carrying neurons were not significantly different from 0.5, indicating that reference and probe color had an equal influence on neuronal responses.
source: As the slopes were not significantly different from 0.5, this indicates that reference and probe color had an equal influence on neuronal responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the regression analysis results.

claim: Divisive normalization was observable in the neuronal population, and as a consequence of this computation, neurons had generally less information about the color identity at load 2.
source: We thus show that DNR was observable in the neuronal population, and as a consequence of this computation, neurons had generally less information about the color identity at load 2.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the divisive normalization analysis.

claim: Information-gaining sample neurons had a slope of 0.19 (R2adj 0.05, F(1,446) = 23.0, p < 0.001, CI = [0.11 0.27]).
source: Sample neurons had a slope of 0.19 (R2adj 0.05, F(1,446) = 23.0, p < 0.001, CI = [0.11 0.27], Figure 5B), and delay neurons had a slope of –0.04 (R2adj –0.015, F(1,62) = 0.08, p = 0.78, CI = [–0.29 0.22], Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a result from regression analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Information-gaining delay neurons had a slope of –0.04 (R2adj –0.015, F(1,62) = 0.08, p = 0.78, CI = [–0.29 0.22]).
source: Sample neurons had a slope of 0.19 (R2adj 0.05, F(1,446) = 23.0, p < 0.001, CI = [0.11 0.27], Figure 5B), and delay neurons had a slope of –0.04 (R2adj –0.015, F(1,62) = 0.08, p = 0.78, CI = [–0.29 0.22], Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a result from regression analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Both slopes of information-gaining neurons were significantly smaller than 0.5, indicating that these neurons were influenced more strongly by the reference color.
source: Both slopes were significantly smaller than 0.5 and smaller than the slopes of the non-informative neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). This indicates that these neurons were influenced more strongly by the reference color, and that the addition of the probe color at load 2 resulted in an unequal interaction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the regression analysis results.

claim: The addition of the probe color at load 2 resulted in an unequal interaction for information-gaining neurons.
source: Both slopes were significantly smaller than 0.5 and smaller than the slopes of the non-informative neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). This indicates that these neurons were influenced more strongly by the reference color, and that the addition of the probe color at load 2 resulted in an unequal interaction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the regression analysis results.

claim: Divisive normalization was computationally responsible for a gain of information at load 2 in a specific subset of neurons.
source: Therefore, DNR was also computationally responsible for a gain of information at load 2, in a specific subset of neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of information-gaining neurons.

claim: The working memory capacity of crows is limited to about four items.
source: In brief, we found that the WM capacity of crows is limited to about four items, and that the two visual hemifields are largely independent (i.e., the number of items on one side does not affect change detection performance on the other side).
evidence: This is a summary of behavioral findings.

claim: The two visual hemifields are largely independent in crow working memory (i.e., the number of items on one side does not affect change detection performance on the other side).
source: In brief, we found that the WM capacity of crows is limited to about four items, and that the two visual hemifields are largely independent (i.e., the number of items on one side does not affect change detection performance on the other side).
evidence: This is a summary of behavioral findings.

claim: Within each hemifield, performance dropped gradually with the addition of a second and third item but remained above chance.
source: Within each hemifield, performance dropped gradually with the addition of a second and third item but remained above chance.
evidence: This is a summary of behavioral findings.

claim: On the neuronal level, there was a roughly 50% reduction in color information when the number of colored squares was increased from one to two in correct trials.
source: Fittingly, on the neuronal level, we found a markedly reduced amount of color information when the number of colored squares was increased from one to two (roughly 50% reduction in correct trials).
evidence: This is a summary of neuronal findings.

claim: The neuronal data suggests that working memory could be conceptualized as a continuous resource that has to be divided between items, rather than discrete slots.
source: This suggests that WM could be conceptualized as a continuous resource that has to be divided between the two items (Bays and Husain, 2008; van den Berg et al., 2012; Wilken and Ma, 2004), rather than two 'simple' slots that would each have the same amount of information irrespective of the memory load.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the neuronal data pattern supported by citations to theoretical models.

claim: The findings are consistent with results of human neuroimaging that report decreased signal amplitude and precision with increasing memory load.
source: This is also consistent with results of human neuroimaging that report decreased signal amplitude and precision with increasing memory load (Emrich et al., 2013; Sprague et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison to other studies supported by citations.

claim: The hemispheric independence observed would fit a slot-like model, in which the hemispheres as a whole act like discrete slots.
source: In contrast, the hemispheric independence we observed would fit a slot-like model, in which the hemispheres as a whole act like discrete slots.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the hemispheric independence finding.

claim: A 'slots and averaging' model could account for graded amounts of information within a limited number of slots.
source: A more nuanced version of the slot model ('slots and averaging'; Zhang and Luck, 2008) could also account for graded amounts of information within a limited number of slots (Fukuda et al., 2010; Zhang and Luck, 2008), as we found here.
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to theoretical models.

claim: The mix of discrete and independent hemispheres with a graded allocation of information between items is comparable to results by Buschman et al., 2011, observed in monkey PFC.
source: The mix of discrete and independent hemispheres with a graded allocation of information between items that we found is comparable to results by Buschman et al., 2011, observed in monkey PFC.
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by a citation.

claim: Recurrent connections between neurons within a hemisphere may reduce item differentiation when multiple items are present simultaneously, creating capacity limitations within the hemisphere.
source: On the neuronal level, recurrent connections between neurons within a hemisphere may reduce item differentiation when multiple items are present simultaneously, creating capacity limitations within the hemisphere (Matsushima and Tanaka, 2014).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by a citation.

claim: A lack of interhemispheric recurrent connections would make processing in the other hemisphere independent.
source: A lack of interhemispheric recurrent connections would make processing in the other hemisphere independent.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation inferred from the data pattern.

claim: Working memory capacity in crows may result from neuronal activity patterns governed by multiple individual items.
source: Like in monkeys, WM capacity in crows may therefore result from neuronal activity patterns governed by multiple individual items.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: Task similarity is very important for cross species comparisons as even small changes in task parameters may introduce substantial differences in neuronal responses.
source: Task similarity is very important for such cross species comparisons as even small changes in task parameters may introduce substantial differences in neuronal responses, leading to potentially different conclusions.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration based on knowledge of comparative neuroscience.

claim: In a task by Lara and Wallis, 2014, neurons in the PFC of monkeys encoded nearly no information about color, but instead about location.
source: In a task similar to the one used here, Lara and Wallis, 2014, have found that neurons in the PFC of monkeys encoded nearly no information about color, but instead about location.
evidence: This is a citation to another study's findings.

claim: The exact task design may determine the neuronal encoding of task relevant information.
source: In brief, the exact task design may determine the neuronal encoding of task relevant information (Lara and Wallis, 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by a citation.

claim: Neurons of NCL can encode a wide range of very different task relevant aspects, like color, spatial locations, rules, and numerosities.
source: Similar to the complex contribution of PFC neurons to WM, neurons of NCL can also encode a wide range of very different task relevant aspects, like color (this study), spatial locations (Rinnert et al., 2019; Veit et al., 2017), and more abstract items like rules (Veit and Nieder, 2013) and numerosities (Ditz and Nieder, 2015).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Attention may play an important role in crow working memory.
source: Our results suggest that attention may play an important role in crow WM.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results.

claim: Capacity limitation became apparent during encoding, as the amount of information at the end of the sample period was affected by the stimulus load.
source: Capacity limitation became apparent during encoding, as the amount of information at the end of the sample period was affected by the stimulus load.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: Adding a second and third item to the ipsilateral stimulus array reduced the amount of color information encoded by NCL neurons that carried over into the memory delay.
source: Adding a second and third item to the ipsilateral stimulus array reduced the amount of color information encoded by NCL neurons that carried over into the memory delay.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: Neuronal activity in trials in which the birds made an incorrect response showed only weak encoding during the sample phase without information maintenance during the memory delay.
source: Furthermore, neuronal activity in trials in which the birds made an incorrect response showed only weak encoding during the sample phase without information maintenance during the memory delay.
evidence: This is an observation from the error trial analysis.

claim: Studies of human working memory have shown attentive filtering during encoding of stimuli influencing working memory capacity.
source: This fits studies of human WM that have shown attentive filtering during encoding of stimuli influencing WM capacity (Bays and Husain, 2008; Vogel et al., 2005; Vogel and Machizawa, 2004), and neuronal correlates of this have been reported for monkeys as well (Buschman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a citation to other studies.

claim: Neuronal correlates of attentive filtering during encoding have been reported for monkeys.
source: This fits studies of human WM that have shown attentive filtering during encoding of stimuli influencing WM capacity (Bays and Husain, 2008; Vogel et al., 2005; Vogel and Machizawa, 2004), and neuronal correlates of this have been reported for monkeys as well (Buschman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a citation to another study.

claim: Neuronal correlates of working memory and attention overlap in PFC neurons.
source: Neuronal correlates of WM and attention overlap in PFC neurons, for example, Lebedev et al., 2004, found that a substantial amount of PFC neurons encode either an attentional signal, or a memory signal, and some (hybrid) neurons do both.
evidence: This is a citation to another study.

claim: A purely mnemonic function of PFC seems unlikely.
source: A purely mnemonic function of PFC thereby seems unlikely.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited literature.

claim: At the population level, neurons of PFC encode both the selection of items from working memory and attention to sensory inputs, rather than just memory content.
source: Indeed, very recently, Panichello and Buschman, 2021, have reported that at the population level neurons of PFC encode 'both the selection of items from working memory and attention to sensory inputs' (p. 2), rather than just memory content.
evidence: This is a citation to a recent study.

claim: The independence of hemifields observed on the behavioral level and in neuronal responses could be related to attention.
source: The independence of hemifields that we observed on the behavioral level (this study and Balakhonov and Rose, 2017) and found in the neuronal responses could also be related to attention.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Adding stimuli in the contralateral hemifield affected neither performance nor information maintained by NCL neurons, whereas additional ipsilateral stimuli strongly reduced both.
source: Adding stimuli in the contralateral hemifield affected neither performance nor information maintained by NCL neurons, whereas additional ipsilateral stimuli strongly reduced both.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings.

claim: The influence of attention on working memory and hemifield independence is consistently accentuated in studies in which attention had to be divided between the two hemifields.
source: This fits the influence of attention on WM and hemifield independence, which is consistently accentuated in studies in which attention had to be divided between the two hemifields (Alvarez and Cavanagh, 2005; Buschman et al., 2011; Cavanagh and Alvarez, 2005; Delvenne, 2005; Delvenne et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The divisive normalization computation may explain the responses of the neurons that gained information at load 2 through attentional processes predicted by the 'normalization model of attention'.
source: Finally, the DNR computation may explain the responses of the neurons that gained information at load 2 through attentional processes predicted by the 'normalization model of attention' (Reynolds and Heeger, 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation to a theoretical model.

claim: When attention is overtly directed to a specific item within the receptive field of a neuron, the divisive normalization computation shifts its weighting of the normalized response toward the response of the attended item.
source: However, when attention is overtly directed to a specific (preferred or non-preferred) item within the receptive field of a neuron, the DNR computation shifts its weighting of the normalized response toward the response of the attended item (Reynolds et al., 1999; Reynolds and Heeger, 2009).
evidence: This is a description of a mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Weighted normalization can produce a difference in the neuronal response to both color identities at load 2, even if the neuronal response was non-informative at load 1.
source: This weighted normalization can produce a difference in the neuronal response to both color identities at load 2, even if the neuronal response was non-informative at load 1.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism.

claim: An attentive process might have enhanced information in working memory at higher loads.
source: Thus, an attentive process might have enhanced information in WM at higher loads.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The animals participating in this study can use attentional cues to enhance their working memory.
source: However, we do know that the animals participating in this study can use attentional cues to enhance their WM (Fongaro and Rose, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to another study.

claim: Attention cues positively affected not only encoding but also the maintenance and retrieval of the information held in working memory, comparable to results from monkeys and humans.
source: The attention cues used by Fongaro and Rose, 2020, positively affected not only encoding but also the maintenance and retrieval of the information held in WM, comparable to results from monkeys and humans (Brady and Hampton, 2018; Souza and Oberauer, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies.

claim: The neuronal recordings offer a mechanistic explanation for the behavioral effects, as clear evidence of divisive normalization governing the neuronal responses tied to working memory capacity was found.
source: Our neuronal recordings offer a mechanistic explanation for the behavioral effects, as we found clear evidence of DNR governing the neuronal responses tied to WM capacity that is in accordance with mammalian models of WM capacity (Bouchacourt and Buschman, 2019; Lundqvist et al., 2016; Lundqvist et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings supported by citations to models.

claim: The loss of information about color identity can be accounted for by divisive normalization when an item is added to a neuron's receptive field.
source: The loss of information about color identity (i.e., neuronal response differentiation between colors) can be accounted for by DNR when an item is added to a neuron's receptive field.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism.

claim: The normalization of neuronal firing rate diminishes the differentiation between color identities, analogous to neurophysiological responses from visual areas and to the PFC during spatial working memory.
source: The normalization of neuronal firing rate diminishes the differentiation between color identities. As such it is analogous to neurophysiological responses from visual areas (Carandini et al., 1997; Reynolds et al., 1999) and to the PFC during spatial WM (Matsushima and Tanaka, 2014).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: The working memory model of Bouchacourt and Buschman, 2019, is based solely on data from monkey electrophysiology, and thus implicitly tied to the layered columns of the neocortex.
source: The WM model of Bouchacourt and Buschman, 2019, is based solely on data from monkey electrophysiology, and thus implicitly tied to the layered columns of the neocortex.
evidence: This is a characterization of a cited model.

claim: The results show that the model of Bouchacourt and Buschman, 2019, also fits the neurophysiology of working memory in crows.
source: The results we report here show that the model also fits the neurophysiology of WM in crows.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the findings.

claim: Oscillations of local field potentials are relevant for how information enters working memory and how it is maintained.
source: Oscillations of local field potentials are relevant for how information enters WM and how it is maintained (Miller et al., 2018), and have been tied to normalization and competition between items in WM (Lundqvist et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies.

claim: Oscillations have been tied to normalization and competition between items in working memory.
source: Oscillations of local field potentials are relevant for how information enters WM and how it is maintained (Miller et al., 2018), and have been tied to normalization and competition between items in WM (Lundqvist et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study.

claim: The oscillatory interplay of the layers and different regions of the mammalian neocortex are important fields of research to further our understanding of working memory.
source: Thus, the oscillatory interplay of the layers and different regions of the mammalian neocortex are important fields of research to further our understanding of WM.
evidence: This is a statement about research priorities.

claim: The oscillatory aspects of working memory are so far completely unknown in crows and their non-layered associative areas.
source: Such aspects are so far completely unknown in crows and their non-layered associative areas.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: No neuron showed persistent activity comparable to those reported by classical working memory studies in PFC or in NCL.
source: We cannot report of any neuron that showed persistent activity comparable to those reported by classical WM studies in PFC (e.g., Funahashi et al., 1989; Fuster and Alexander, 1971), or in NCL (Diekamp et al., 2002b; Veit et al., 2014; Veit and Nieder, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about what was not observed, with citations to studies that did observe persistent activity.

claim: The lack of persistent activity may be reconcilable with some contemporary models of working memory that implement 'synfire chains', where individual neurons fire sequentially to bridge temporal gaps.
source: This may be reconcilable with some other contemporary models of WM. One major type of those models implements 'synfire chains', where individual neurons fire sequentially (and transiently) to bridge temporal gaps and maintain task relevant contents (Rajan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation to a model.

claim: Sequential transient activity has been reported in posterior parietal cortex of mice performing a T-maze task that required working memory for cued spatial locations.
source: This has, for example, been reported to be the case in posterior parietal cortex of mice performing a T-maze task that required WM for cued spatial locations to be maintained (Harvey et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a citation to another study.

claim: The transient activity of neurons reported in this study might fit into synfire chain models.
source: The transient activity of neurons that we report (Figures 2 and 3A) might fit into such models.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Recent work has shown that the sensory areas of mammals and birds show remarkably similar circuit organization.
source: Recent work has shown that the sensory areas of mammals and birds show remarkably similar circuit organization (Stacho et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study.

claim: Higher-order associative areas involved in working memory, like the LPFC in mammals and the NCL in birds, have distinctly different architectures.
source: However, higher-order associative areas involved in WM, like the LPFC in mammals and the NCL in birds, have distinctly different architectures (Stacho et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study.

claim: The fact that differently organized areas like LPFC and NCL produce strikingly similar physiological responses points to shared computational principles.
source: The fact that differently organized areas like LPFC and NCL produce strikingly similar physiological responses points to shared computational principles.
evidence: This is an inference from the findings.

claim: Modeling work suggests that the competing working memory capacity models can be accommodated into a unifying framework based on theoretical neuronal information sampling.
source: Modeling work already suggests that the competing WM capacity models can be accommodated into a unifying framework based on theoretical neuronal information sampling, where stochastic information sampling (assumed for continuous resource models) can account for item limitations better than fixed information sampling (assumed by the slots and averaging models) (Schneegans et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a modeling study.

claim: Divisive normalization is considered to be a general, canonical computation of the nervous system, present in evolutionarily distant phyla, for example, fruit flies and monkeys.
source: Similarly, DNR is already considered to be a general, canonical computation of the nervous system, present in evolutionarily distant phyla, for example, fruit flies and monkeys (Carandini and Heeger, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: The computations by individual neurons that result in working memory capacity limitations are virtually the same in crows and monkeys.
source: Our results show that the computations by individual neurons that result in WM capacity limitations are virtually the same in crows and monkeys, highlighting a further aspect of WM that is similar between these animal groups (Nieder, 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the findings supported by a citation.

claim: The results were in line with different modern models of working memory that implement divisive normalization to explain capacity.
source: Ultimately, our results were in line with different modern models of WM that implement DNR to explain capacity (Bouchacourt and Buschman, 2019; Lundqvist et al., 2016; Lundqvist et al., 2011; Schneegans et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by citations to models.

claim: The data presented cannot carry a definitive conclusion about which of the different models fits best.
source: However, the data we presented cannot carry a definitive conclusion about which of the different models fits best.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the study.

claim: The study shows that mammalian models of working memory are in line with working memory in birds, which implies that fundamental aspects of working memory are shared between these animal groups.
source: We do, however, show that mammalian models of WM are in line with WM in birds, which implies that fundamental aspects of WM are shared between these animal groups.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the findings.

claim: The different intricate neuronal architectures that carry out the computations in monkeys and crows have likely been shaped by convergent evolution into systems that yield similar cognitive performances.
source: Together, all these facets of crow WM capacity suggest that the different intricate neuronal architectures that carry out the computations in monkeys and crows have likely been shaped by convergent evolution – into systems that yield similar cognitive performances.
evidence: This is a conclusion about evolutionary convergence inferred from the findings.

claim: The systems may share the same basic mechanisms and thus limitations.
source: The systems may share the same basic mechanisms and thus limitations.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the findings.

claim: Further investigation into the oscillatory dynamics of working memory in the avian brain may elucidate if birds also share the prominent limitation of a tradeoff between flexibility and capacity.
source: Further investigation into the oscillatory dynamics of WM in the avian brain may elucidate if birds also share the prominent limitation of a tradeoff between flexibility and capacity.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: Two hand-raised carrion crows of 2 years of age served as subjects in this study.
source: Two hand-raised carrion crows (C. corone) of 2 years of age served as subjects in this study.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: All experimental procedures and housing conditions were carried out in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and were authorized by the national authority (LANUV).
source: All experimental procedures and housing conditions were carried out in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and were authorized by the national authority (LANUV).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.
